Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I refer to the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos). The hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) should have as much character and fortitude as the hon. member for Montmorency.
I have more, but I talk some sense.

The hon. member for Sarnia is well trained; he knows when to say aye.
I think it was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), in an earlier incarnation as Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, even before I was here, who coined the phrase "industrial development strategy". He started work on it then. 1 do not know how many years ago that was, but we are still waiting. In any event, this Minister of Finance says he is going to do it. How is he going to do it? By restraining government spending and holding the deficit in check. Then the government talks about energy development.
It is totally baffling how the Minister of Finance could on Monday, January 12, after seeing the impact of his October 28 energy policy, still maintain that there will be energy development in this country anything like what is needed. Obviously the Minister of Finance is not an ignorant man. He is not dumb. He is aware of what is happening. But because it does not fit in with the politics of the moment to acknowledge it, we carry on with this policy of the big lie.
We hear things such as, "This is what we are going to do. We are going to have energy development." The minister knows that is not what is happening. I know that his officials, below the deputy level, are scurrying for cover and saying that they did not have anything to do with that October 28 document, that they did not see it. We hear them say that it was done by EMR, the deputy, and one or two people around him. No one in finance had any say, and there are some honourable people in that department who would have liked to have had some say in producing a budget for this country. However, for some reason or other that task was turned over to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and he produced that body blow.
Unfortunately for the Minister of Finance, he is the one who will have to pick up the political credit for it. He will find that unemployment this year will be far greater than he had expected or planned. His officials never really had a chance to look at that energy policy. I gather no one in government did, other than the department of energy. But the Minister of Finance is the one who will have to pay the political price of accounting for that increased unemployment, the increased drain on the public treasury for its subsidies on the imports, and the increased strain on the dollar because of our increased balance of payments deficit, and on and on. The Minister of Finance will have to bear that cross put on his shoulders by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who somehow conned him into reading his energy policy.
Economic adjustment is another thing to which the minister is committed. What does economic adjustment mean? Is it another Department of Regional Economic Expansion? Do you remember that, Mr. Speaker? The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was supposed to cure regional disparity in Canada. How many years have we had of that department? The truth of the matter is there is something more fundamentally wrong with Keynesian policies or the Keynesian approach. It has a fundamentally inflationary bias built into it. To begin with, it calls on governments to run surpluses when the economy is overheated. That is almost an impossibility in a democracy. It is almost impossible for a government to run a surplus because the number of spending plans dreamed up by politicians, bureaucrats and others are absolutely overwhelming, and no matter how overheated the economy gets, the reality is there is some just cause out there for money to be spent on. It is almost impossible to run the kinds of surpluses needed to balance off the deficits that are incurred in terms of stimulus.
On the other side, it is fundamentally inflationary in instinct. The theory is that governments, by spending more, putting more money into the economy, stimulate demand and bring on jobs. However, there is a time lag. When you stimulate demand, the first thing that occurs is the price goes up. The first thing that occurs when there is increased demand is a price increase. After the price goes up, you get increased supply. The increased prices bring on the new production and you are up to new levels. You have this inherent inflationary bias in the process, and that is what is wrong with the New Democratic approach. They are talking about more government spending, stimulating demand and thereby helping inflation. Perhaps, but in the process this would raise inflation to a new high. That happens everywhere.

The investment tax credit idea for certain regions in Canada is an idea which is about as original as it was in 1963 when it was first put forward by Walter Gordon.
It has been introduced time and time again as an attempt to solve the problems of regional disparity in Canada on a very temporary and ineffective basis. But nowhere in the budget do we see any discussion of the philosophy behind the Income Tax Act. Nowhere do we find a discussion as to what the general purpose or thrust of the policy is. Nowhere do we find an attempt to say that in 1967 the Carter commission put forward certain recommendations and in 1972 the tax reform bill was passed in order to achieve certain results, this is where we stand now and this is where we would like to go for the 1980s. The fact is we are further away from the principle that a dollar, no matter how it is earned, should be taxed equally and fairly. We are further away from that principle than we were in 1967, when Mr. Carter put forward his recommendations in the royal commission.
I point out to the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen)- and I would like to hear him announce this at one of those meetings I am sure he holds regularly in his riding-that there are 24 Canadians who earned over $200,000 in 1977 who paid no tax. I would like to hear him tell that to the workers in his riding. The member for Sarnia can tell that to the petrochemical workers in his riding. If they tried to do that, Mr. Speaker, they would be thrown in jail. These are 24 Canadians who legally, because of the loopholes we have in our tax system, paid not a penny in taxes.

Since the elimination of the estate tax in 1971, it has had the effect of a lump sum transfer of $4.5 billion to Canada's wealthiest citizens.

Current estimates of wealth can only be approximated since it is hidden behind a statistical curtain, but we do know that personal income has increased by over three times and that personal savings have increased by over six and a half times since 1970. The point is that we cannot continue with a series of minor income tax proposals which fiddle here and fiddle there without recognizing that we face a major crisis, what I call a "crisis of fairness", in our tax system. As long as the government is prepared to say that there is a whole realm of wealth which can be transferred from one generation to the next without taxation, it will be those people whose taxes will continuously rise and whose purchasing power

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INITIATING INDEPENDENT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of initiating an independent commission of inquiry to investigate the serious deficiencies within the administration of search and rescue services on Canada's west coast.
He said: It is most appropriate and, I believe, long overdue that we should have an opportunity to debate in this House a motion which is of such life-saving importance. I set down motion No. 26, Mr. Speaker, because events have shown in recent years that there is indeed a serious lack of co-ordination and there is a question of administrative inefficiency which must be addressed regarding the relationship of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to the delivery of search and rescue services, particularly on the west coast.
In March, 1980, I wrote to the Minister of National Defence and to the Minister of Transport urging them, in the wake of the Lee Wang Zin sinking on December 25, 1979, to initiate such an inquiry. Letters of response from both ministers, which I received later that month, refused to consider initiating such an inquiry. I subsequently submitted this motion to the House and today I want to present some of the circumstances, centering particularly on the Lee Wang Zin tragedy, but bringing up other numerous cases of what 1 believe to be administrative incompetence when it comes to saving human life.
In reply to my letter of March, 1980, both ministers indicated that they were engaged in an interdepartmental review of the co-ordination of rescue facilities between their two departments. In fact, Mr. Speaker, that review was commissioned by the former Conservative government under the then minister
January 16, 1981

of national defence, the minister of transport and the minister responsible for marine transport. That review was to have been completed in the spring of 1980 and I was advised by those ministers that I would receive copies of the review within weeks. Now, nine months later, I still do not have notice of the findings of that review.
The basic problem is that the principal administrators of search and rescue, the decision-makers and politicians here in Ottawa, are apathetic about this crisis and about the loss of human life, which usually takes place in cold water.
This is a very serious problem for the people of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, especially those who make their livelihood on the Pacific coast waters or who use those waters regularly for recreational and other purposes. This includes fishermen, pleasure boat operators, the B.C. ferries, coastal cruisers, those engaged in shipping, towing and flying, to a large degree.
I want to make it clear this afternoon that it is not my purpose to accuse or criticize individual persons who operate the Rescue Co-ordination Centre in Victoria or those who man the search and rescue services generally. These people are doing an excellent job in many respects and have saved many human lives. We commend them for that. The problem is that they are governed by bureaucratic directives and orders from above. The system is at fault. The attitudes among senior decision-makers within that system is what 1 call the "admiralty approach" to search and rescue, rather than the blood and guts approach which is required in order to get to the site of a tragic accident in time to save the lives of people in the water.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, a report which summarizes the findings and recommendations of the jury at the inquest on the Lee Wang Zin sinking in December of 1979 when the lives of 30 Taiwanese crew members were lost in an overturned vessel. The Department of Transport did not attend the scene until 38 hours after the first SOS signal was received.
I should like hon. members to imagine themselves for a moment in the position of a young Taiwanese sailor just having left the port of Prince Rupert after loading ore, on his way home to Taiwan to greet his wife and children. He is awakened at five o'clock in the morning, notices that the ship is heaving and rolling heavily, not in its usual fashion, is suddenly thrown into a catastrophic overturn, his bedding thrown around the cabin. He worries and wonders whether a distress signal has been sent. He calls for his friends, searches around the lower reaches of the vessel for them, feels the heaving motion of the ship from the underside of the berth where he is trying to hang on for dear life. He grows fearful and cold, his teeth chatter, he grows numb while he wonders, waits and hopes. Nothing happens. He waits for an hour, maybe half an hour, maybe three hours, perhaps 24 hours. He grows more and more numb, sleepy and weak. He gradually subsides, never to see the light of day again.
That was the tragedy that the crew of this vessel faced, that the rest of us can pretend to ignore. They were trapped within the overturned hulk of a seagoing freighter on December 25, 1979.
Search and Rescue Services
Meanwhile, at the Rescue Co-ordination Centre in Victoria, the distress signal had been heard and reported. It was a clearly coded distress signal, "SOS-EEC". The men at the co-ordination centre, however, took almost an hour to identify the ship. This is not necessarily their fault because they did not have an up-to-date copy of the international directory of ships' call signs and so could not identify the vessel. The identification is important because that is the only way the ship's name could be determined and thus its point of departure and the course it was taking.
At the coroner's inquest which took place in January and February of 1980, evidence was presented that a coastguard helicopter located in Prince Rupert, only 60 kilometres from the scene of the accident, did not become airborne until three hours after the first SOS signal was received. It was not until Boxing Day, 32 hours after the mayday signal, that the first coastguard vessel arrived on the scene. It had been undergoing a refit and had to be put back together before they could proceed to sea.
No attempt was made by the Rescue Co-ordination Centre to seek the help of Rescue 15, a group of 40 volunteer boaters operating out of Prince Rupert. If they had been asked, they would have been willing to respond to the first mayday signal. Indeed, they did obey a coastguard directive in the book of rules which prohibits self-dispatching. They stayed home. What kind of directive is it that prevents people from going to the assistance of their fellowmen?
A tugboat, the Cindy Mozel could have responded within an hour of the mayday call, not 32 hours, but it was not called. In fact, no general mayday call was relayed on all frequencies after the signal had been translated.
At Canadian Forces Base, Comox, the Labrador helicopters are normally on two-hour standby. That is how long it takes to get them in the air during off hours. It is a policy dictated by Ottawa and applied across Canada. On that day, however, it would have taken three and one-half or four hours to get the aircraft up there and then they would have had to refuel at Prince Rupert. The helicopters were not ready. They are reported to have been under repair at the time.
Eventually the Rescue Co-ordination Centre called for a United States helicopter based in Sitka, Alaska, because the United States had the equipment and the trained search and rescue personnel available.
Why do I call for an independent inquiry, Mr. Speaker? It is in part because other startling testimony was presented to the inquest which is documented in the coroner's report. The duty watch officer was not called to testify. This testimony was given by the commanding officer. The coastguard maintained that the crew died instantly and that therefore any rescue attempt would have been futile. What kind of an attitude is that, Mr. Speaker, to decide the time of death before the facts are known? There was a long distance assumption that there would be no ship in the area and therefore the relay of the mayday message was deemed to be unnecessary. This was testimony at the coroner's inquest. The Rescue Co-ordination Centre decided to delay help on the assumption that conditions

January 16, 1981
Search and Rescue Services
were too rough. If you do not know where the vessel is or you only have a rough idea, how can you assume that conditions are too rough? The circumstances of the Lee Wang Zin are tragic indeed. 1 do not want to finger any particular individuals in these departments; the matter is in the past. But the threat of error rests in a whole series of problems, including inadequate equipment, delays in getting started, errors of judgment, procedural mistakes, refusals of offers of assistance from other vessels in the area, improper telephone numbers and communication problems.
These difficulties are not restricted to the Lee Wang Zin tragedy. They are common to many accidents in recent years on the west coast, most of which go unnoticed here in Ottawa because they involve fewer lives. But in any event, the problems are similar. They boil down to a question of distance and time. Can we get to the scene fast enough and do we have the required rescue equipment in order to get into the water to keep those people alive before it is too late?
This blood and guts attitude, characteristic of the British lifeboat system, of the volunteer system and of the Canadian Armed Forces personnel when they jump out of a helicopter into the water, and this eagerness of people to be involved in saving another person's life is what is important in mounting an effective search and rescue service. It has been characterized by one well-known and not too popular spokesman on the west coast that Canada's search and rescue operations are managed as follows: "They have one guy doing a job and ten guys slinging paper".
I want to tell you now about a 17-year-old girl named Sandra Klein. A year or two ago Sandra and her father were patrolling in the Gulf Islands. They were called to a scene of a burning sailboat. They were closer than any other vessel. She travelled single handedly in a 17-foot Boston whaler at speeds of 25 to 30 knots across 17 miles in 27 minutes. She arrived at the scene of the burning sailboat. There was no one on board. She spotted a floating form in the water. At the same time she noted adjacent to her on the scene there was a navy vessel, the YMR-4. This navy vessel did not have a small enough boat to launch into the water. The crew were clustered in the bow looking at the floating casualty. Sandra Klein jumped into the icy water. She supported the man and applied mouth-to-mout'' resuscitation and applied it continuously as they were both lifted from the water by the navy vessel. That is an act of valour. Subsequently Sandra's act of valour was acknowledged by the Governor General by the granting of an award to this 17-year-old girl for her efforts in saving a man's life while the navy looked on.
I think this speaks of the change of attitude which is required in the delivery of search and rescue, particularly on our west coast.
Just this morning Lieutenant-General K. E. Lewis, Commander Air Command responsible for search and rescue at a conference in Ottawa in response to a question said, "Search and rescue is a highly visible and high profile operation."
Therefore, decisions as to the involvement of Armed Forces Reserve units, or for that matter auxiliary assistance, were a matter of political consideration.
In his written presentation to the conference Lieutenant-General Lewis commended west coast search and rescue for assisting in the saving of 519 passengers' lives on the Prinzen-dam which burned in the Gulf of Alaska in Canadian waters last fall. His written presentation in part states:
It is of interest to note that 442 squadron was notified at 0500 on a Saturday morning and within 3 hours was able to launch two Buffaloes, two Labrador helicopters and a full medical team.
1 submit that two hours is not enough. It is too much time. When people are in cold water, particularly in winter weather, they are susceptible to hypothermia which is fatal within a half an hour, and a two-hour standby is far too long.
The government spent almost $3 million last year on west coast search and rescue to handle 4,200 rescue calls. That is approximately 12 calls each day year round, including winter time. The budget allows some $650 per incident in terms of funding for the main search and rescue exercise. The volunteers who are trying to organize along the lines of the British lifeboat brigade who use their own vessels and equipment are reimbursed $30 per incident.
These people recently approached the government requesting an increase to $70 per incident. That is one-tenth of what the gold-plated system consumes. They wanted only $70 per incident to meet the fuel expenses, to buy a radio, to provide rescue equipment on their private craft, but it was refused. These people are ready and willing to assist in search and rescue, but the government appears to provide very little assistance. Indeed, it treats these individuals as amateurs in some respects. Statements have been made. One individual was told when he was asked to stand down and not attend the scene of an incident that the taxpayer would rather have a government vessel do the work. That is typical of our society these days, isn't it, Mr. Speaker? Where is the spirit of voluntarism going?
Most individuals who arc willing to participate in these rescue efforts are experienced on the water, whether they are fishermen, salvagers, pleasure boat operators, ferry captains, tow boat operators or others. These people can provide a valuable service if encouraged. The reluctance of national defence, coastguard and rescue co-ordination centres to utilize the services of Rescue 15, a group of 40 volunteers in Prince Rupert on Christmas Day a year ago should be proof that something is wrong within the system. As I have already said, the coastguard has issued a directive ordering volunteers not to respond to calls unless they are dispatched. It might cost the government another $30.
1 had a most enjoyable week in Wales visiting British lifeboat stations, touring the watch stations, and the radio monitoring systems. Their rescue boats are maintained just as fire engines are maintained by a volunteer fire department. They polish brass, but they are there to provide beach watch and marine safety training to their communities. These stations are spaced ten to 20 miles apart along the coast. They
January 16, 1981

can get to the scene of an accident in ten or 20 minutes, not two to four hours. This closely linked network of volunteer operated rescue stations has to be developed in Canada on both coasts working in co-operation-not being obstructed- by the formal search and rescue services administered by the Department of National Defence and the Department of Transport.
We have just learned that a new rescue station is to be opened at Ganges on Saltspring Island. That station is 12 miles from the main shipping lane. It has cost over $400,000 in start-up capital. It is three miles from the open water and the main shipping lane is where most of our major and tragic marine incidents have occurred in B.C. Why was that station located 12 miles from the main shipping lane? That makes no sense. Why have we no float-equipped rescue aircraft with paradrop teams equipped with scuba gear available and on standby? Why do we have hovercraft that cannot move in a 70-mile-per-hour wind? Why do we have 100-foot cutters when we need more small fast boats with low freeboard to get to the scene of a floating person whose life needs to be saved?
I see that my time has come to an end. I wish the ministers were present today. 1 had been advised that they would be. However, I want to urge them to initiate an independent commission of inquiry, not another government review, into the whole state of the delivery of search and rescue services on the west coast where the city of Vancouver is located, the second busiest port in North America, second only to New York. We have in excess of 200,000 pleasure boaters, 5,000 or 6,000 commercial fishing boats, and many hundreds of thousands of people on the water the year round. Their lives are more important than the gold braid or anything else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) on an excellent presentation and on making some very valid points on a very worth-while motion. I certainly hope that there will be sufficient time to vote on this motion.
The question which we must address in terms of search and rescue and the outline which the previous speaker gave concerning the tragic events surrounding the Lee Wang Zin are certainly very pertinent. However, it is history, and what is important now is to learn the lesson and to try to rectify the situation which led up to the incident. I should like to suggest that the first lesson to learn with the Lee Wang Zin is that one ounce of prevention is worth a ton of cure. That was a rust bucket which was sent to sea out of Queen Charlotte after loading in conditions which should never have occurred. A flag of convenience was deliberately set up so that the owners would never have to compensate for an accident. The first thing to remember is that we have a long-term commitment to the prevention of accidents at sea and in the air. That is the first order of business.
The second major flaw in the Lee Wang Zin incident is the fact that that ship was 12 miles offshore, within easy reach
Search and Rescue Services
and flying distance of a helicopter. When the Department of National Defence, in spite of all their communication problems, launched their helicopters, they were unable to provide rescue service for those people. They went there simply to pick up the bodies, if they ever did get there. The first aircraft to go were the Buffalo. After three hours in the water, anybody found would be either dead or in very bad shape. You cannot rescue anybody out of a Buffalo. You have to be able to deliver a helicopter.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the first priority on the coast of British Columbia is to distribute along the coast the five helicopters which have been committed to Comox in such a way that there is an hour or less flying time between that helicopter and any area where an incident might occur. Both Boeing-Vertol which produces the helicopters used by the armed forces and Sikorsky which produced the helicopter at Prince Rupert, state that the costs to locate those bases around the coast of B.C. and refit the helicopters to be operated on those bases would be well under $10 million. In a proposal which I submitted for comment, I suggested that three helb copters remain at Comox, one be placed at the Canadian Armed Forces station at Holberg at the north end of Vancouver Island, and one at the Canadian forces station at Masset, and the Sikorsky air force helicopter be refitted for marine rescue service, be seconded to the armed forces for crewing and be used as a helicopter primarily for search and rescue out of Prince Rupert, with an effective, trained crew on it. If that were done along the coast of British Columbia and southeast Alaska, it would mean that there would never be a marine incident or a medical evacuation less than one hour's flying time away.
I myself and most of the people I have spoken to in this business-and I have travelled from Alaska all the way up and down the coast of British Columbia and through the state of Washington looking at coast guard search and rescue facilities-believe that helicopters are the key. You have to be able to deliver a crew to the site who can effect the rescue and provide the services there.
Next, we must consider the business of volunteers. We use helicopters at Comox and Buffalo aircraft during the spring, summer and fall months for searches of downed aircraft, and this consumes thousands of hours of search time. Two summers ago two aircraft were lost, one between Kamloops and Vancouver, which is a massive area, a mountainous terrain, and the other one was lost somewhere in the Terrace area. These two aircraft were searched for by the Canadian Armed Forces aircraft and also by a group set up by the provincial emergency program, an air patrol.
Eventually they found the aircraft at an absolute fraction of the cost, with more aircraft in the air and trained people working under supervision of search masters, and they did an excellent job. The point made by my colleague, the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta, is valid, that, in addition to placing those helicopters along the coast of British Columbia, the hard edge of a rescue service is delivered within an hour.

January 16, 1981
Search and Rescue Services
The second point is that a volunteer service, particularly a province-wide civil air patrol which can participate, be organized. They can get on the job as soon as the ELT goes off, as soon as the emergency is put in. They can begin the search and they can start covering the territory. It takes the armed forces, in some cases, 24 hours before they get a ground base and a search pattern set up, the aircraft refueled and ready to go. Then there is the tremendous expense of those searches to be considered.
Mention was made of the Klein family, Horst, his wife and daughter. The points made about them were absolutely true and, in fact, understated the event to the nth degree. There was a number of difficult rescues in which that family had participated. It is astounding. They were the first people on the scene when the ferry, the Queen of Alberni, was grounded at Active Pass. They were the first ones there to render assistance, and what is amazing is that they did not receive any information from the rescue co-ordination centre. They picked this information off a commercial broadcast on CKNW and then wound up in Active Pass as the first people to render assistance on the scene.
Sandra has been involved in a number of diving exploits which, unfortunately, have not been as successful, but these were difficult and dangerous commitments for which she was awarded a medal of substantial merit. What is really required, of course, is a marine organization across the entire coast of British Columbia which is properly equipped and given adequate recompense for out of pocket expenses. You cannot run a 180 on $30 for an event. You need so much an hour to cover fuel, the wearing down of your engine, oil, maintenance, and what not. If the government were to realistically pay these people to go out on air and marine searches, it would save thousands of dollars.
Many of the pilots who engage in those search operations are former members of the armed forces. They are expert fliers and they have had tremendous experience in searching and mountain flying. They have the qualifications to do the job. The people who are involved in Rescue-15, in the group in the Queen Charlottes, in the group on the central coast out of Bella Bella, in Powell River, in Campbell River, in the north Island, in the Gold River, all the way up and down the coast, are represented by people with tremendous qualifications and experience in the marine environment, whether they are fishermen, tugboat personnel or experienced mariners.
Then there is this problem of adequately equipping volunteers. The Canadian Marine Rescue Association is in its formative stage. It has not jelled yet, but it is certainly under way. I think more consideration should be given to the kind of training, assistance and budget which the government could provide, and especially to the equipment given those people. If it is inadequate, they cannot do the job.
I will give you just one example. Most of the people who work out of Bella Bella are quite familiar with the marine environment and with their own area. The minute a problem comes up in the area, if someone is lost-and this happened in the middle of winter last year during the election campaignthey come to the rescue. We were stranded there because of freezing cold winds building up ice on the aircraft which, as a result, could not fly. A couple of people were lost. Those people managed to set up a search locally. They checked all the places where they were likely to be.
The armed forces sent a helicopter, but it was not equipped with a radio which would allow them to talk to the provincial emergency program on the ground. As a result, they searched the whole area which had already been searched and they were not able to check the places where it was likely the people were lost. It is an unfortunate situation, but in these cases the first priority is for helicopters. We have to distribute them along the coast in order to cut down the response time. The second thing we must do is strengthen our commitment and make an investment now to save thousands, if not millions later on, in the volunteer service there.
I have made some very definite statements on the events surrounding the Prinzendam. I think that anyone would admit that had the oil tanker not been there to provide a base from which the aircraft could operate, 500 people would have been lost at the bottom of the sea. It was a happy incident or coincident that an oil tanker was there to act as a helicopter platform to work from and to evacuate the people. That, in my opinion, was the only thing that saved the lives of the people on that ship. Otherwise they would have been at the bottom of the sea. The Lee Wang Zin incident is history and we have to learn from that.
Out of that Lee Wang Zin incident particularly we must learn, and I would congratulate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for being open and frank in that regard. I think the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta was a little bit in error regarding the person in charge of the rescue co-ordination. He did not wind up having to testify. It was a junior coastguard officer who wound up testifying. The officer in charge was never exposed to a public inquiry at the coroner's inquest as to why this occurred. The Department of National Defence did its own in-house investigation. 1 attempted on many occasions to obtain that report. They refused to give it out. The Minister of Transport did make the report public as well as supplying staff to testify at the coroner's inquest. This gave people an insight into what had actually happened.
In the rescue services and marine pollution response of the coastguard of the United States, they have two kinds of interesting aspects and the first relates to helicopters. If somebody is missing, a boat is immediately dispatched to where they were anticipated to be. A phone search is made to make sure the missing person had not landed. This is immediately instituted. At that point, three people go out to the helicopter and the helicopter is warmed up. If there is not a firm response that those people have been found in 30 minutes, that helicopter takes off and heads off to the point.
That does not happen in Canada. We wait hours and hours sometimes before those things are launched. They should be on
January 16, 1981

24-hour standby and they should be looking at a 30-minute launch time or as soon as they can clarify a likely position.
The other thing the Americans have that we could learn from is their simulation exercise. The Lee Wang Zin accident was absolute chaos. They did not know whether they were punched, bored or chewed out by the rats as it came out in the final analysis. We could learn from those mistakes and we should learn from them.
I was not able to take part in an observation exercise in the United States, but I know they run simulation programs. They simulate an accident and bring in people who are involved from the coastguard, the navy, the air force and others from the public who have expertise. They examine the situation on closed video criticizing how the rescue program was handled and then make suggestions as to how they could improve this kind of response. This hones the edge to a very effective one.
In southeast Alaska and on the south coast of British Columbia, especially around Victoria and the southwest part of Vancouver Island, your chances are excellent of being rescued by an American helicopter if you run into difficulty, but your chances are not so good if you are being rescued by a Canadian helicopter which is probably stationed no greater distance away.
I should like to qualify those remarks. I know personally of events and incidents in which members of 442 Squadron at Comox have been involved. It is acknowledged even in the American coastguard that Canadians are capable of more activities than even they are. For example, if someone is in the water, no one from a U.S. coastguard helicopter will go into the water after him. You either get on the hook or you are in big trouble. They may get a navy diver to get in after you. The fellows in the 442 have training second to none in the world and their accomplishments have been excellent.
Our big problem relates to inadequate equipment. Resources applied to the program are inadequate. Consequently, the job cannot be done. This is basically a government problem involving helicopter distribution, response and the way we treat volunteers. We should invest in that very valuable resource, the people who want to participate.
The third priority is co-ordinating government resources. There are 14 federal government helicopters on the coast of British Columbia. There have been occasions when we could not get one into the air to look for someone. Even if we can get one into the air, often it cannot get to the scene in time.
On a beautiful night in the September before last, there were two people on a fish boat off the north end of the Queen Charlotte Islands, not too far from Prince Rupert. The moon was bright and the water was calm. One fellow fell overboard while trying to make a repair to the side of the ship. They radioed in and that was it. They never got a helicopter out and they never did find him. On that occasion, in beautiful weather, they were unable to respond.
We have 14 helicopters and something like 200 federal government vessels on the west coast of British Columbia, and we are not making effective use of those resources. I do not
Search and Rescue Services
want to beat on the issue any longer about the Canadian coastguard helicopter at Prince Rupert, but it is an excellent machine and, in my opinion, it ought to be converted immediately for search and rescue. It ought to be seconded to the Canadian Armed Forces to be used for coastguard purposes, except when there is a search and rescue emergency at which time it should go out on that, without question, with a fully trained crew capable of finding and rescuing people.
Let me make just a few more points before I conclude. A lot of people in British Columbia tend to have a very negative response toward these facilities because of fragmentation, poor use of resources, and the inability to deliver a rescue platform in an effective time and I suggest it stems from small things like this.
Two weeks ago there was a phone call from people responsible for assisting British Columbians during the time of disasters such as flooding. There were areas in my riding which could not be reached by this provincial emergency group. They phoned the Canadian Armed Forces and asked if it could send a helicopter because they were unaware of what had happened to the people in the area. All communications had been cut off, but they knew there were extraordinary flooding conditions. The first thing the people in the Air Force asked was: "Who is going to pay for this?" That was the first word out of that mouth on the phone: "Are you authorized to pay for this?" 1 pay for that helicopter, everyone here and everyone in this country pays for it. The reason we pay for it is to have it available to respond immediately to an emergency situation. The first thing that should be done is the helicopter should be airborne immediately, go directly to the area and later there should be consideration about the transfer of funds.
How do British Columbians feel about the federal government's rescue resources and the services provided? When that is the first question asked, we do not feel very good about it, especially if you have watched a number of people die unnecessarily in the water.
I have been beating away at this point for two years. I have produced two reports and a basic outline for discussion. I have also produced a study into helicopters and the cost of placing them out, again for discussion. 1 think over a period of time the government's attitude has been changed. The opinion of former minister Otto Lang was that rescue services at sea are voluntary services provided for centuries by other ships at sea. From that point, we have seen a change. The government has undergone a helicopter upgrading program. The government has made a commitment to buy a 170-foot vessel and a commitment to station a number of 21-metre vessels in the area. The government has put in place an inshore rescue boat program which has answered about one-fifth of the incidents which have occurred off the coast of British Columbia and has undertaken an education program directed toward that very area of prevention. The government has also involved more extensively its other resources. The vessel traffic management system is now an effective resource. All of southwestern British Columbia, with a combination of aircraft, hovercraft and vessels, has access to these services. So the government

January 16, 1981
Search and Rescue Services
deserves some credit. It is aware of this issue but not in the way Otto Lang was. I think it is seriously concerned.
However, this government has not gone far enough or fast enough. People are still in jeopardy because of poor rescue services. Helicopters and their proper distribution are vital, and the government has been receiving letters from every municipality and regional district along the coast asking that that program be put in place. The government must make use of voluntary services in order to make this program effective. Finally, we must get to the point where we are co-ordinating more effectively. We should not be empire-building in separate government departments. There should be more effective coordination. I suggest that would come about through a more efficient use of resources. There should be closer co-ordination between departments and the designation of another primary respondent other than the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne). There should be simulation exercises in which members of the public and trained professionals participate so that they can criticize what is going on.
I will sit down in the hope that the proposal of the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta will be accepted.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INITIATING INDEPENDENT COMMISSION OF INQUIRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on behalf of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), who intended to be here, but was prevented from being here in the last couple of hours because of weather conditions in the part of the province of Quebec he is visiting today. 1 want to tell the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) that the minister had fully intended to be here, until a couple of hours ago.
I am pleased to rise on behalf of the minister and to make some comments in relation to the subject before the House. I think I have said on a previous occasion in relation to the exercise we are involved in now that I find the private members' hour to be perhaps one of the more valuable periods provided for in our Standing Orders. In the last 40 minutes, I have heard more thought-provoking suggestions from my friends across the floor than we hear in other debates in this chamber.
Let me say on behalf of the minister that any suggestion by a responsible citizen that any important government service, particularly one dedicated to the saving of life and the reduction of suffering, is deficient in its administration or operations is one which must be closely examined. The motion before the House certainly implies such a situation, and the reaction of the government is, of course, one of concern.
The Canadian forces, with their high readiness posture and ability to respond fairly rapidly in emergencies, are charged with the task of the operational co-ordination of rescue services. These services are provided from four rescue centres situated at Halifax, Trenton, Edmonton and Victoria. The Department of National Defence also furnishes air resources
to each region, including special aircraft, helicopters and trained crews. Other defence aircraft, the primary task of which is not search and rescue, frequently participate in searches as a secondary role, as do aircraft from other government departments and those provided by many civilian pilots across the country.
The Department of Transport is the other major partner in this activity. The coastguard provides marine specialists in the co-ordination centres and vessels for marine operations. Crews and vessels from other departments are also available as required.
I mention these details in order to show that search and rescue cannot be handled by any one organization but must, if it is to be efficient and not prohibitively expensive, take advantage of all suitable vehicles the owners and operators of which are willing and available to assist in the endeavour.
It is a matter of record that in the past 12 months the people at rescue co-ordination centres and in operational search and rescue units across the country have responded to about 10,000 requests for assistance. It is a tribute to the knowledge, experience and dedication of those personnel that such a job can be done, and done so well. Their jobs call for very rapid evaluations of situations, often involving scant details and committing valuable resources which could well be more urgently needed elsewhere at the drop of a hat and risking their own lives to save those of fellow human beings.
This is the daily lot of search and rescue practitioners because accidents at sea and in the air have an uncanny habit of occurring in the most forbidding terrain, on rough seas and generally in adverse weather conditions.
Accidental loss of life under any circumstances is tragic. However, we must face the reality that regardless of the number of resources assigned to our national search and rescue program, it is not always possible to save all the lives, as much as that is our objective.
It is with that sense of reality in mind that following a major government review of marine search and rescue in 1976 two major decisions were taken which are now proving their worth. The first of these was to form an interdepartmental committee on search and rescue to advise ministers on policy, planning, resources and effectiveness. It is jointly chaired by members of the Department of National Defence and Transport Canada and involves officials from a number of other government departments.
The second decision was that the government would embark on a rational, sensible and credible continuing program to improve substantially search and rescue procedures and resource availability right across the country.
In order that the government might control the management of search and rescue regularly, the committee was directed to provide for review by ministers an annual plan in which the need for primary search and rescue response is identified.
Since 1976, five such plans have been produced. As a part of their development, a detailed analysis of the needs of each region is performed by local specialists who are familiar with
January 16, 1981

prevailing conditions. These regional analyses are then reviewed by the appropriate departments of government, resulting in a consolidated national plan with recommendations for improvement. This plan is then reviewed by the interdepartmental committee to which I referred. It is ultimately referred to cabinet for decision.
Let me outline very briefly a few of the more important initiatives which have resulted from these two decisions I have mentioned since 1976.
First, the government directed an in-depth review of the co-ordination centres, which has recently been completed. A number of recommendations are already being implemented. I refer to such recommendations as functional relationships between Canadian forces and Canadian coastguard personnel in the centres, streamlining of procedures and changes to regional boundaries.
Second, the coastguard has developed an ongoing five-year acquisition and replacement program for search and rescue vessels, which is working out very well.
Third, while it is not possible to buy literally off the shelf a rescue helicopter which will meet particularly unique Canadian needs, in 1976 the government directed that the majority of the existing rescue helicopters be modified to provide improved foul weather day and night capability. The initial phase, involving improved communications, navigation equipment and external illumination, was completed three years later, in 1979. The second phase, which is now in progress, is providing longer-range capability for these helicopters, a much superior rescue hoist, radar to facilitate poor weather search and better radio communications with vessels. This will be complete by 1984.
Fourth, in 1977 the North American search and rescue business suffered a major setback when an unforeseen hazard surfaced in the batteries of the emergency locator transmitters.
These devices, which provide early warning of distress for both aircraft and ships, had to be withdrawn from universal use in the aviation community. As a result of persistent work by the interdepartmental committee, I have recently been advised by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that he anticipates these devices will again be universally carried in light aircraft by the end of the present year. Provided regulations are rigorously enforced, this will be the single most significant factor in speeding up rescue in air distress. It will save lives and reduce suffering. It will also save flying hours expended each year searching for crash locations not pinpointed by the emergency locator transmitters to which I referred. This in turn will make crews and aircraft available to respond to other distress calls.
Fifth, Canada is participating in the international search and rescue satellite-aided tracking project. When emergency locator transmitters are in full use, this project will enable early warning of distress and quick localization of ELT signals. The system will begin testing and evaluation with the launch of the first satellite in 1982. When this ambitious
Search and Rescue Services
project becomes operational, it will reduce significantly the loss of life and suffering involved in air and marine disasters.
The Department of National Defence has examined the adequacy of air response to marine and air incidents across the country. While concluding that current location of resources, their numbers and state of readiness are adequate, certain areas for improvement have been identified. In April, when considering the 1982-83 plan, cabinet will decide how best these improvements can be made.
I should like to use my remaining time to address more particularly the concern raised by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta. I thought it was important by way of general background to inform the House of some of the initiatives which the department, in collaboration with other affected departments, have been taking especially since these two important decisions of 1976 which underlie the present search and rescue thrust. Cabinet has been concerned with the situation on the west coast because the marine activity level is high and in the northern portion of the west coast there has been a small but significant concentration of marine distress incidents which is increasing annually. In December, cabinet approved a recommendation in the 1981-82 plan for a detailed review of the region. This will soon be conducted by members of the Canadian forces and the coastguard.
Our operational capability on the west coast is already high, and the following two examples clearly illustrate its flexibility. The first example has already been referred to by both previous speakers, the Prinzendam disaster from which 519 people were rescued without any loss of life in very adverse weather conditions. It is significant that in the southern portion of the region the coastguard hovercraft at Vancouver frequently responds to distress in United States waters. Similarly, Victoria can and does obtain the services of United States coastguard helicopters on standby at Port Angeles, Washington and Sitka, Alaska. This bilateral arrangement is both effective and economical.
On December 27 and 28 the squadron on Comox was asked to provide two helicopters to assist in the rescue of over 100 people caught in the flooding at Squamish, British Columbia. This work was hazardous, especially during the night. The rescue was successful because crews were available at short notice, because of their skill in aircraft handling under extreme conditions, and because of the competence of the rescue technicians who had to work in diving gear at the end of lifelines and in total darkness.
Also, I should mention at this point that the rigorous analysis of all factors involved in search and rescue incidents on the west coast has enabled the rescue organization to cope very effectively with unusually high peak demands over the last few years. In particular, I refer to the herring roe season when through a combination of education, prevention, and enforcement and judicious deployment of resources, we have been able to reduce considerably the number of lives lost during this relatively new and hectic activity. I believe this is

January 16, 1981
Search and Rescue Services
further proof that the administrative system instituted in 1976 is bringing concrete results by ensuring a flexible response to changing requirements and a better utilization and co-ordination of all available resources; not only those of the government but also private resources which happen to be in the vicinity of an emergency.
In spite of the high confidence the government places in the operational capability of the people and resources on the west coast, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Transport have examined independently the peculiar problem of northern British Columbia, in particular the Prince Rupert area, in so far as search and rescue are concerned. These examinations have confirmed that the assignment of dedicated coastguard vessels to this area this year and in following years will provide for effective responses to maritime distress.
We on this side of the House are not insensitive to the significant and tragic loss of life which has occurred off the west coast. At the same time, it has been determined that some of the loss could not have been avoided, even with unlimited resources. Nevertheless, a closer study of the requirements for air resources is necessary and will take place early this year.
The regular activities of the interdepartmental committee, the annual review of search and rescue by ministers, the significant progress achieved over the past four years by this process, and the record of achievements by search and rescue personnel, their vessels and their aircraft, do not reflect any need at this time for an independent commission of inquiry. On the contrary, current government policy is already ensuring regular, orderly and effective progress toward improving the probability of rescuing the passengers and crews of aircraft and vessels in distress situations. Therefore, the government must conclude that the proposed independent inquiry would be unnecessary, costly and disruptive to the continuous review and upgrading process 1 have described. For this reason I want to inform the members who have spoken in this debate that it is not the intention of the Department of National Defence to entertain such a proposal at this time.
In conclusion, the House will understand that my first responsibility during the past few minutes was to speak on
behalf of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) and to inform members of the thinking of the Department of National Defence on the issues raised by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta. If time would have permitted, I would have addressed myself, as a Newfoundlander, to the subject of search and rescue as it affects the Atlantic coast. There are a number of issues in that regard which need to be aired, but I decided to discharge my first responsibility and respond as directly as possible to the concerns raised by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta and the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). Let me assure both members that their concerns will be scrutinized by the Minister of National Defence and others who are concerned about this important subject. If something needs to be pursued, I assure these members that it will be.
